Welcome to the Classroom!

Whatever your level of experience, if you have a query, this is where you'll find many people to help you answer it. There's no such thing as a stupid question, and you can be sure that if you wonder about something, there are others who wonder the same and will be glad you aired it. There's lots of homework set for you to do. If you'd like help getting started with it, feel free to post your first couple of examples here for critique, before you do the rest and put them in your journal.

To perpetuate the "Traders helping Traders" philosophy, once you've learned concepts and understand them fully, you're encouraged to share what you've learned with those who come behind you. This is not just good for them, but will help concrete your own understanding of the material, so after you've learned by learning, you'll then learn by teaching!

None of us have the time to answer queries by PM, so please use this room to learn together as a group. We're sure you'll find friends for life in here!

If you're here to learn, post a chart of your mistakes. Indicate where you took the trade, why, and your targets. Let the forum add their input. At the very least, start a trading journal and record the history of good and bad trades. Figure out why and how the good ones worked and why the bad ones didn't. On a side note, it is vey difficult to replicate live trading on a demo. A demo is good to try new concepts etc but it will never teach you the mindset needed to enter and exit trades. However, if you learn supply and demand trading well AND trust it, it helps takes those wicked emotions away.

Good question. I'm a big fan of correlating pairs. I think it serves as a good indicator. First is to realize how one pair correlates to another. Then you watch the levels like you would any other trade. For example, this past Friday, on the GU & EU moved closed together. Watch when one pair reacted at a level then other followed. Also look at the crosses for a good indication. The EURGBP was a good indictor on Friday. AU and NU was also an easier pair to correlate. There's a benefit to trading the pair that slightly lags, just make sure you're trading the levels according to that pair. Meaning that, let's say, demand was 50 pips away on the leading pair and only 25 pips away on the lagging pair, target the 25 pips if trading the lagging pair not the 50 pips as indicated on the leading pair. Hope that helps.

It's always best to be aware of which currency is going to cause the turn

If you want to, say, sell GU, you should know whether it's because of the dollar getting ready to rise, or the pound to fall Looking at the dollar pairs will tell you if it's the former, in which case you'll look for the pair with the best setup and room to move

If not, look at the various pound pairs, and if GBP is in Supply all round, you'll know that the turn will be due to oncoming pound weakness, making it the ideal time to sell

In essence, always be aware of who is about to turn the market

Hi friends, I have a question. What is your opinion?

Hi Sunny,

That's a good question!

A decision point in itself is powerfull. The word say it all "Decision", meaning that someone decided if price was too cheap or too expansive at that particular moment in time.

Once a decision has been made, you will always see some kind of follow through however you have to look at the whole picture in order to see where price is likely going to go. Let's say that price is at demand and a decision point was made to take price south. So what happened? Someone decide that price was too "expansive" and they want to see price going down but you should ask yourself where price is likely to go from there... Is there another fresh DP just bellow/above price? Is there enough room for price to move? Could it be that price went down so that they could buy back at a better price?

To answer all this questions, you deffinately have to look at HTF's and see where price is and where it's trading to.

Hope this helps, Mel

Rosa, are you asking about best entry procedures, or where to place stops on a runner?

Hi Rosa, so your question is about set ups and stops. As i understand it you prefer to trade off H4....good option for reducing screen time.

Your set ups should be very accurately traced from history on the remaining higher time frames.That would be D1, Weekly and Monthly.

Make note of S/r and S/d static prices levels(horizontal lines). Draw them onto the higher tf...then go down to H4. Most platforms will automatically save what you have drawn. Visually check how your drawn levels relate to H4.and the current pa there.Trend lines are best drawn on the tf that you are trading off....to give a sense of gradient and an additional guide for your stop loss.

Stops are subjective to pa but more importantly to your risk reward ratio. ( please see danandsuecos article on stop losses.)Typically you should only be risking 2-3% on a trade so if you cannot find a trade at that rr you should not take the trade imo.Subjective to pa you should be looking for a stop at next available s/r drawn from higher tf, ideally.

I use same tf levels and/or nearest (to ratio) dp...indecision candles are a favourite of mine.

As mentioned above trend lines can give additional confirmation on setting your s/l, particularly when confluence of static levels occurr ( please read Markepedia on confluence)

I hope this serves to help. Good luck with you trading.

Balance occurs when neither sellers nor buyers are motivated to move price beyond a range. We see this balance on our charts in the form of a consolidation or range. These occur on all time frames. Eventually either sellers or buyers will become impatient and move price beyond the range. If there is extreme imbalance as shown here then the breakout will be sudden and violent. These violent moves out of these consolidations or clusters create new demand or supply. In this case new demand was created. So now we are very interested in this area when price moves away for some time then returns.

When price breaks from a consolidation, range or cluster whether of short or long duration we have the makings of a potential DP. A clear break from a cluster with price moving clearly up or down with follow through is key. If there is no follow through then there really isn't a decision. If price stalls and moves back then IMO no decision was made. Price needs to engulf the previous price action and clearly break away.

I chose this area in the chart below to illustrate something. Notice 1 and 2 are clear areas where price broke up with a bullish engulfing (BE). The first or lower BE broke out of a larger cluster than the one in BE 2. But price IMO did not truly make a decision to go much higher. Price stalled before getting to 3. If price had broken above 3 then that to me is a real decision because price would have engulfed the bearish price action to the left. In this case price did not engulf the bearish price action to the left so no real decision. Now this is in the context of the time frame shown.

Having said all that above if you look at this on LTFs then in the context of LTFs these areas would probably be significant DPs.

Also I want to stress again that DPs occur on all time frames. You may be able to clarify the area on a LTF. Also more DPs will occur on LTFs.

Hi HRT,

If you are new to Supply and Demand than I suggest to just try to trade the fresh zones. Just make sure that you know what the leading directions are from Higher Time Frames zones.

Start your weekly analysis by looking at where price is on the HTF's. For example What is the direction price is trading at the moment on Monthly, Weekly, Daily, 4h. Are we trading towards Supply or Demand? Did we just left Supply or Demand?

Once you become comfortable at trading only fresh zones, you than can start looking at tested zones.

I encourage you to get some screen time too. Draw your zones of intrest and watch how price reacts to it. This is a great way to learn more.

Once you have your zones in place, look at the approach, is price compressing up towards your fresh supply/demand than it's a good thing. Let price show you what it wants to do and then trade in synch with it.

Also, you really want to look at the potential target. If you have a fresh supply zone and there is not a lot of room for price to move, than as a beginner you can skip the opportunity and look for a beter place to trade elswhere.

If you are new, I suggest you don't risk real money while learning. You can learn on a demo accout but yet treat it like it was real money. This is where you will get your discipline from. If you are really serious and dedicated about your future trading career, you got to be disciplined and put a lot of time and dedication to have this working. The good news for you is that you already found out that supply and demand is an important part of trading, this gives you an edge over other traders but like I said earlier there is a lot more to look at than just pure s/d but you'll discover all this set by step.

So try to digest all the above and than make a decision. Are you willing to put the time and effort that is needed to become succesfull or are you not.

Wishing you all the best anyway. Mel

Yes, in essence, it would be pretty accurate to say that price is either in consolidation or in a pole. We're certainly safest trading from the extremes of either. Just look at when price breaks an high or low, with an FTR; see the rejection which so very often occurs from the new FL on return. when this FL eventually breaks, price has entered the pole. Some may trade this break, but they must be ready to suffer DD right back through the flag, and sometimes even slightly beyond. Hence, for safety, it's usually best to let price break and form an FTR which we can trade from on return. The tg is usually the base of the pole, but if price starts showing signs of compression through the pole, watch out for possible support/resistance flips along the way, especially if price hadn't hit its target before the flag broke back into the pole.

There are very many variables in this scenario, so to draw a set of charts for it would mean explaining every single PA setup there is. So I urge you to look through your charts and try to make sense of these words.

this is called whipsaw engulfing. 1. Cluster (where supply and demand are balanced) near supply.

2. Cluster resolves north and becomes demand. Many novice breakout traders go long without knowing that they are going right into supply. 3. Cluster is engulfed south by big sellers in supply. Ignored cluster now becomes supply. 4. Need to go short when/if price retraces to cluster. You may find DBD in Sell Zone in lower timeframe to refine your short entry.

The great benefit of a forum such as this is that everyone can accelerate their education, not only by doing their own work and having it assessed (an absolute necessity as you can only learn things your way), but by looking at the work of others and seeing how that is assessed. Hi tradingjedi - this may not be the answer you are looking for, but may help you understand why price did what it did. In the context of the price action as visible on the 15M chart at that point in time (i.e. ignoring HTF levels etc), this is what I see:

1 and 2 are swing highs (i.e. price too expensive) 3 and 4 are swing lows (i.e. price too cheap) 5 price starts to turn, possibly in response to ignored supply to left - but who cares -because price does not move up and engulf anything 6 price pulls back to whatever tentative demand rests at 5 and then quickly shoots up and engulfs 1 and 2 - i.e. the Decision Point to engulf was in 6. Your initial entry (my blue box) was barely a RBR and not the origin of the decision to engulf - hence why it was ignored on the way back to fill the rest of the orders at 6. At the moment you can see the residual demand created by 5 and 6 being chewed up.

I hope this helps a bit.

The main focus of this analysis is on identifying where the key zones are in the PA. have been studying a lot of the journals here and pulling it together as best I can.

An engulf had already taken place and price had capped nicely, and the CP back up to the edge of the zone was a confluence indicator that price might be headed south when it eventually reaches the opposite end of this upper zone. Price moves between the opposite ends of the zones, and then decisions are made. The pause at the top demarks the a decision - price stalled, brielfy, and it could have gone north and returned into the zone and would have been an FO. But it doesnt. Its form manifests as price drops south and this becomes our FTR.

Down in the middle, we have a flag limit and I also pick this up as an FTR. Price hhas halted here, and very well could have reversed back up. But it doesnt. It bases, and then its form again is made manifest, and it is decided it is still too expensive, in the middle of the value curve here. So this is another FTR.

Down at the bottom I marked out what I see as being a key area of price action, and there is a nice FO DBR out and back in from underneath. This movement causes a nice RBR which engulfs the recent high. And in fact the box here could have started higher. After the engulf, one sign prices might be headed higher, the pullback comes back into the zone and bounces of a support level. This itself engulfs the last high that was formed (not shown), but the engulf had already happened, and readying to take a position had already ensued.

Naturally, price makes its way to the opposite end of the zone (flag) and bounces back in from the FL. A few attempts are made, and indeed there are a few short trades here that I havent shown to avoid over cluttering the chart. The nice thing about all of this is that price comes back to where it wants to be - the origin. Within this area an engulf north happens (on the right at the bottom of the chart), and price bounces (naturally) back down from the FL. We have a double bottom and double top. Notice also just to the left, price makes a little CP as it rises, before price plummets. This is a nice movement for the pro money because it allows them to take the liquidity on the way down so that they can load up for the big move up to the top zone that they are look to. So price bounces from that small FL and makes its way back down to the demand zone that was created by the FTR all the way on the left. This double bottom is capped, and for sure this was a place to take an aggressive long position. From here price engulfs the latest high before retreating slightly (FTR). This base at the edge of the zone causes a new makjor move up. Also notice on right at the top edge of the magenta rectangle, a little blip that I point to indicating an FTR. At the edge of this zone, a stall unfolds, but it is decided it is too cheap, and price rises strongly. Nicely, price makes its way all the way to the top, to the FTR that caused the move down right at the left of the chart. A nice TT trade or such like down from this FTB to the FTR could have been taken.

When price falls under the supply at the FTR, where is its target? The FTR that caused the move up - that tiny blip/FL/FTR at the edge of the flag down at the bottom. See the second chart - it shows what happens when price returns to the source.

For me there are four types or returns, RT or FTB with normal respect to the zone. FO which engulfs and rejects the zone.

ENG which engulfs and continues in the direction of the engulf. A fourth return is the fail to return.

FO vs ENG When I see an engulf and wonder whether it is a FO or a ENG continuation I'll look for; the strength of the reaction after the FO/ENG 1... cp back to fresh zone (weak reaction), perfect to tighten your SL or if you're confident add another position. 2... lq engulfing fresh zone/dp/fl instantly (strong reaction), you should get out of your trade and wait for your entry signal 3... cplq (wedge... ) continuation after the FO, which should now be named ENG instead of FO. 4.... instead of reacting to the FO/ENG price could also simply form a DP/FL only to advance with strong LQ 5.... price can also cp back to the fresh levels only to consume them and hit you with LQ (hate it when that happens), but most of the time you will see a S level turn D before that happen, vice versa D turns S.

So in general I look at the reaction + where the nearest zones are to counter this reaction (defensive range after effort) and I also base my conclusion on what the HTFs tell me, ofcourse.

Not sure if I'm one with the best understanding of FTR's, but I'll give you my 2 pips regarding this.

I'm not saying that those areas should be ignored out of hand, but as they become older, perhaps less real attention should be paid to them when compared to what's happening right now. The fresh liquidity could be just what Pro Money needs to push prices further along if they aren't looking to book profits and turn. Well there are various methods to trade for example touch trades or unfolding PA trades.

In my experience supply and demand zones have higher probability to work out when entries are made in the direction of engulfing waves. When trades are taken against trend, S/D zones are less likely to work out or give just a minor pull back often causing losses. Now if price engulfs down and reaches demand zone which is inside higher time frame demand zone lets say looking at H4 and price enters demand zone of Weekly chart then it becomes a different story. For example on H4 it might appear that price is waving down and engulfing down, but looking at weekly it might actually just retrace to demand zone of waves up and engulfs up. Higher time frames are stronger than lower ones so always need to keep them in mind where price is.

The harder part is to enter a trade right, when waves are rising engulfing prior supply zones they rarely come/retrace back to new created demand zones and price runs away creating feelings of being right but not being in the market.

What I would suggest to try is to go over and study all the information posted here, apply it to charts and see how it works, go over some of major journals see how they have applied that same information to their trading. And then just trade, trade and trade. After gaining experience your method will start to develop.

Understanding the words of a new language is critical if you want to speak it, even more so if you want to be able to read it. I want to be able to "read the market" but I confess that I find the lingo confusing sometimes, especially when working through homework (which I will be posting to my own journal shortly.) In this post I'm going TRY to define some of the important words of the language of the market that are used at RTM. I tried to write this for someone with no market knowledge or experience in the hopes that I will learn by thinking through the concepts and taking little to nothing for granted.

Disclaimer: these definitions are based on the current understanding of someone learning "marketese" and may be completely wrong! On some definitions I've included sources but feel free to chime in on any of these.

Supply (S or SUP): sell orders that put pressure on price to fall. When Supply exceeds Demand, price falls. When Demand exceeds Supply, price rises.

Demand (D or DEM): buy orders that put pressure on price to rise. When Demand exceeds Supply, price rises. When Supply exceeds Demand, price falls.

Rally-Base-Drop (RBD): a 3-step process whereby: 1. demand exceeds supply and causes price to rise (Rally); 2. supply and demand find balance and price stabilizes (Base); 3. supply exceeds demand and causes price to fall (Drop). The return to the base is often tradable.

Drop-Base-Rally (DBR): a 3-step process whereby: 1. supply exceeds demand and causes price to fall (Drop); 2. supply and demand find balance and price stabilizes (Base); 3. demand exceeds supply and causes price to rise (Rally). The return to the base is often tradable.

Support-Resistance Flip (S/R Flip): a price point or zone that limits price's move downward, then breaks and later limits price's move upward.

Resistance-Support Flip (R/S Flip): a price point or zone that limits price's move upward, then breaks and later limits price's move downward.

Cap on Price (CAP): the base of a RBD or DBR. This is where price is limited from further upward movement in a rally or further downward movement in a drop. Source: Caps on Price article, If'd video on Caps, and even the article's name: "... RBD/DBR". Noticing the name alone was actually an aha moment for me last night.

Pole: the sharp rally or drop that precedes a Flag.

Flag: the base of a RBR or DBD. This is where price pauses to "catch its breath" before continuing on in the direction from which it came. Flags are also the "framework" for Flag Limits." Source: previous understand and the Flag Limit article and its name: "...DBD/RBR". This too was an aha moment for me last night.

Flag Limit (FL): the edges of a Flag. Price often rallies from the bottom Flag Limit and drops from the top Flag Limit before eventually breaking outside of the Flag altogether. The Flag Limit that was Engulfed before price left the Flag is often tradable when price returns.

Failure to Return (FTR): the same thing as a Flag Limit. Source: Ifmyante on FF speaking to Les_Paul - link: bit.ly/1pt3VRN I don't understand the "simple" part (yet), but since FTR's = FL's, should we drop using/trying to understand 1 of the 2? Or am I oversimplifying and misunderstanding If and there really is a difference between FL's and FTR's?

Engulf (ENG): two possible definitions: 1. the consumption of a Demand zone when price is coming from a Supply zone. The return to the Supply zone is sellable with the expectation that price will drop beyond the consumed zone that was Demand; 2. the consumption of a Supply zone when price is coming from a Demand zone. The return to the Demand zone is buyable with the expectation that price will rise beyond the consumed zone that was Supply. ** In either case, if there is no Engulf, then there is no Failure to Return. Source: Ifmayante on FF replying to Chica - link: bit.ly/1f9MJxg

Compression (CP): indecision in the market where price ranges between Supply and Demand. With most (if not all) orders removed from the range, price can easily move through it the next time it arrives at the Compression.

Price Action Zone (PAZ): the tradeable range between 2 Failure to Returns. Price moves between Failure to Returns until sufficient orders enter the market to Engulf a Failure to Return. At that point price moves between the Failure to Return that was just Engulfed and the next Failure to Return beyond it, which is another Price Action Zone.

Thanks in advance for your time and thoughts!

As I mentioned in my post of definitions, I find our lingo a bit confusing sometimes so I'm hoping you all can help out. Here are some examples: Chart 1 is an EA H4 with Caps marked in pink and Flags boxed with yellow (I stopped marking Flags part way through because I had enough to ask my questions.) I currently understand Caps to be RBDs and DBRs and Flags to occur in DBDs and RBRs. But it seems that the action that we can take when price returns to either is the exact same.

For instance chart 2 is a zoom in on the green box. Point A is a pause (aka: base) in a DBD. Immediately below it at point B there is a Cap that comes at the bottom of a pole (aka: a drop.) Yep, you've got just about every FTR in there. The term "FTR" can be applied to pretty much every swing high in a downtrend (for example). If you can find the key FTRs, those where price has broken something significant prior to forming the FTR, those are the places to look to take trades from the "tip" of the FTR.

I've chosen not to draw in every FTR on this chart, but only those where price has broken something significant (the black lines showing previous lows). At these line, price has the choice to go up, or keep dropping. This gives them their significance -they are previous decision points. In each case, price breaks them, and it's very last effort to go higher is the tip of the FTR. I just roughly marked these in yellow. Each of these area will have significant points of supply in them, and we look to trade down from these, based on price action in a lower time frame.

I like the 3rd one down, it has broken 2 significant levels (the second, more minor level, is not marked in. It's about 1.0932)

Well, and keep in mind I am still not a successful trader, I see it as the engulf in a signal that price will turn. In this USDCAD example, that entry I labeled #1 was the first time any supply had been engulfed on the way down after the 30M FL was engulfed. I see this happen a lot at market turns. I invite you to do the same. Pick a time frame and mark off the turns in the market (not spikes but turns). Often I see one of 3 things

a) something local engulfed, retracement to source and then price leaves never to come back b) something local engulfed, retracement plus fake out and the price leaves and comes back for a QM c) something local engulfed, retracement, plus fake out, price leaves, comes back, QM fails and a diamond happens

Whether it is a, b, or c depends on what is to the left usually. But I do see those scenarios happen all over the place.

Try watching M1 turns for example. At the top of a move, a marker/flag usually appears. When that is engulfed south, that is usually the reverse signal. Time to look for an SR flip, locked in demand or some other structure to reverse on.

An example from USDCAD today. Red lines are levels that get engulfed followed by returns to source. Again, this is just how I see it and I am still learning. I also wanted to add that this does not work everywhere on the chart. M1 levels get broken all the time. But an M1 level that forms in HTF supply, then gets engulfed south, well, that is something to pay attention to (in my opinion).

I think I discovered my answer to the fakeout question. If we think about a supply zone above the market and price faking out a previous high into that supply zone, we're inclined to think about it in terms of the supply zone relative to the previous high. So we're thinking "Why is the fakeout going to this supply zone above the high?", but if you turn it around and think "Why is this high below this supply zone?" it makes more sense. If when the price was rising initially, before the first high was made, the ITs sell early, before their final destination then they create that high, below our supply (fakeout) zone. So when price fakesout, really it's not reaching some extra supply zone, it's reaching the intended supply zone, but they've structured it in such a way as to deceive traders. Traders think the high is the final destination of price, but price is set up for a final (fake) move up to the supply zone above the high, to be quickly crushed and turned around.

In case people still wonder what's FTR and what's FL. Let this diagram clear the confusion, and I am not inventing something new, I am just applying what I have learned from the articles in Marketpedia

FTR = Failure to Return. I would actually prefer a more precise technical term. Because Failure to Return can be applied on any Fresh SD zones, i.e. after a zone is created, price has not returned to test it, so arguably any Fresh level = Failure to Return.

The definition of FTR vs FL, according to the Marketpedia articles can be summarized in the following diagram:

So essentially, an FL is created AFTER breaking a key barrier, and FL is drawn from Point 1 to Point 2. Where FTR is the MPL of the FL on this SAME TIMEFRAME.

The next question I see many people have asked is, where do we look for trades? Is it at DP (decision to break), or at FL, or at FTR?

MasterTrader Harry, basically put this to rest. according to him, - If after the creation of FL, price comes back to test the FL within a short period of time, then the FL has a high chance of turning price around. - However, if price does not come back, instead it leaves the area and go on a significant consolidation period, by the time it comes to this area, the FL is no longer a reliable trade location.

So here is my takeaway from Harry's words: if price comes back after a long consolidation period away from the area, I would look at the FL as a FO level, and pay attention to the DP just beyond it as the area that has higher chance of turning price.

I have also seen the word DP (Decision Point) causing confusion, because based on normal English definition, a DP is just Decision Point, and open up any charts, every point on the chart is a decision, every second there are decision to buy and sell by market participants. But in the spirit of RTM, my understanding is that DP is the 'kink' or 'pause' BEFORE the break of a key barrier. Whereas FL is the 'kink' AFTER the break of a barrier.

So DP = Kink, FL = Kink, FTR = Kink but in a lower time scale than the parent FL.

I feel it's like this, although the term FTR isn't used anymore. - A Kink is a FTR. - A FL is a Kink and therefore a FTR. - A kink/FTR might be a FL, but only if the engulf making it a FTR, hits it's target.

To explain a little bit deeper: a FTR, failure to return, isn't a specific part of the kink or the FL, it's the whole of the kink or FL. Say price moves up, but goes down briefly. There's some sort of barrier and therefore price doesn't retrace any deeper, ergo, fails to return, and goes back up. This whole move is, or rather: was, called the FTR. It's simply not the time yet for price to be turned but these kinks do represent some barriers.

As Edge said, it is of critical essence to have a deep understanding of what the kink and/or FL does and why.

@Trab Trading: I think you are correct in saying that you can also enter a trade a bit deeper into the FL. Doing so, you'll minimise the E to SL part of your trade, making it a higher R trade. I think I'm safe in saying that your SL would stay put at the same place, but your entry point moves closer to it, minimising your risk and maximising your reward. A FL remains a FL and doesn't need any refining when talking about entering a trade. You either do that at the edge of the FL, which is the safest point in terms of probability that your order is getting filled, or at the MPL of it. No need to get more specific than that when explaining a trade, because those are the only two possible points of entry. Strictly speaking, you could enter anywhere of course but we're not being taught that, for good reason

I have taken new notes, and arrived at this new definition of FTR. So FTR is no longer the MPL of FL as presented in the article written by Les_Paul in Markepedia.

Now, FTR is drawn exactly the same way as FL, referring to the diagram below. Point 1 = Furthest Advance AFTER breaking the Key Barrier to the left Point 2 = Deepest Retreat AFTER breaking the Key Barrier to the left Point 3 = Price has to move beyond point 1 in order to have an FTR

The key difference between FTR and FL is: FL = FTR that has hit a TG!

Now, I hear you probably screaming in exhaustion now - why can't you guys just stop talking about FTR!!!?!!!

But there is a reason, because there is a 'gap' in the definition of FL. The rule says we cannot draw a FL until a target is reached (i.e. price reach an opposing FL). So if we cannot draw FL, that means we cannot trade FTB to a level that look like an FL?

So we have seen price reacting to FTR, we have also seen price reacting to DP (i.e. a pause/indecision before the break of a barrier). Now if we scrap the concept of FTR and DP all together, we need a FL concept, comprehensive enough to explain these phenomena we saw on the charts every day.

Therefore I urge you and IF to define the new language of RTM, let there be no confusion when we discuss about FL/DP/FTR in the future, if we have to scrap DP/FTR out of our day to day vocabulary, we need something new to replace them.
